messages.subject: Spatial mixture multiscale models in R-INLA?
messages.subject_clean: Spatial mixture multiscale models in R-INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm interested in running a spatial multiscale mixture model which accommodates for a scale effect by sharing both CH and UH simultaneously following the work by Aregay et al  (model 4 in https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26923178 ). Aregay used WinBUGS to specify their model. My data are areal data with ~3400 clinics, nested in ~250 subdistricts. Running the Aregay model in BUGS will take an enormous amount of processing time, if it is even possible. So is it possible to run a similar model to that of Aregay using R-INLA? If so, I would be grateful for any suggestions of examples/papers/tutorials which may be helpful in specifying the model in INLA? I'm fairly new to INLA.

Alternatively is it possible to run a multiscale BYM2 model with PC priors in INLA? If so, any examples/suggestions would once again be appreciated.

Regards,
Harry

messages.subject_clean: bimodal posterior mean distribution after including spatial random field
messages.body_plain:
dear all,

I have applied a glm with a spatial random field in INLA, my response are presence/absence,  modeled as binomial dsitribution. I also run simulations to get the marginal posterior mean distribution (using inla.posterior.sample function). However, I noticed that I ended up with very strange posterior distributions, majority of the 1000 simulations (for one data point) are zeros and ones (i.e. bimodal), see below).

in the meantime, I run the same data using a glm with the same set of covariates, excluding the spatial random field. The estimated coefficients are different than the INLA result, due to missing spatial effect. But I do get a more normal-like distribution of posterior mean.

Can someone help me to explain this strange observation?

Thanks

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] bimodal posterior mean distribution after including spatial random field
messages.body_plain:
Dear Lisa,

The sd's range from 3 to 4.4. That *is* huge in case of a biniomial distribution. The 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles for a normal distribution are -1.96 * sigma and 1.96 * sigma. So if sigma is 4, these quantiles are about -8 and 8.

Let's assume the fixed effects alone yield a probability of 0.9. This is qlogis(0.9) = 2.2 on the logit scale. Add the 2.5% quantile random effect (-8). You end up with -5.8 or a probability of plogis(-5.8) = 0.003. So in a binomial context, a random effect with sigma = 4 is very powerful.

Best regards,

messages.subject: Bug in multiple likelihood demo
messages.subject_clean: Bug in multiple likelihood demo
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I found a bug in the first multiple likelihood demo (and presumably the other example below it) at http://www.r-inla.org/models/tools#TOC-Models-with-more-than-one-type-of-likelihood.  Specifically, it appears to me that the demo assumes intermediate variables are still present in the environment, even if the inla call looks like it only needs the final data.frame.

Here's the first example above, verbatim:

##  Simple linear regression with observations with two different
##  variances.
n = 100
N = 2*n
y = numeric(N)
x = rnorm(N)

y[1:n] = 1 + x[1:n] + rnorm(n, sd = 1/sqrt(1))
y[1:n + n] = 1 + x[1:n + n] + rnorm(n, sd = 1/sqrt(2))

Y = matrix(NA, N, 2)
Y[1:n, 1] = y[1:n]
Y[1:n + n, 2] = y[1:n + n]

formula = Y ~ x + 1
result = inla(
        formula,
        data = data.frame(Y, x),
        family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
        control.family = list(list(prior = "flat", param = numeric()),
                            list()))

This runs as expected.

However, if you run it again with a few small changes that seem like they shouldn't matter, I get an error:

##  Simple linear regression with observations with two different
##  variances.
n = 100
N = 2*n
y = numeric(N)
x = rnorm(N)

y[1:n] = 1 + x[1:n] + rnorm(n, sd = 1/sqrt(1))
y[1:n + n] = 1 + x[1:n + n] + rnorm(n, sd = 1/sqrt(2))

Y = matrix(NA, N, 2)
Y[1:n, 1] = y[1:n]
Y[1:n + n, 2] = y[1:n + n]

df = data.frame(Y, x)

remove(Y)

formula = Y ~ x + 1
result = inla(
        formula,
        data = df,
        family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
        control.family = list(list(prior = "flat", param = numeric()),
                            list()))

Error in eval(parse(text = formula[2]), data) : object 'Y' not found

The issue is that the formula doesn't know how to find "Y" because there is no "Y" in the df data.frame, but rather two columns, "X.1" and "X.2" that are autogenerated from Y.  (It's not better if you do df = data.frame(Y=Y,x=x) as you end up with "Y.1" and "Y.2").  The fact that the original example runs tells me that formula is finding Y in the global environment and not through the data = df part of the inla call.

A fix that works is to change the formula to formula = cbind(Y.1,Y.2) ~ x + 1.  Full working example below:

##  Simple linear regression with observations with two different
##  variances.
n = 100
N = 2*n
y = numeric(N)
x = rnorm(N)

y[1:n] = 1 + x[1:n] + rnorm(n, sd = 1/sqrt(1))
y[1:n + n] = 1 + x[1:n + n] + rnorm(n, sd = 1/sqrt(2))

Y = matrix(NA, N, 2)
Y[1:n, 1] = y[1:n]
Y[1:n + n, 2] = y[1:n + n]

df = data.frame(Y = Y, x = x)

remove(Y)

formula = cbind(Y.1,Y.2) ~ x + 1
result = inla(
        formula,
        data = df,
        family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
        control.family = list(list(prior = "flat", param = numeric()),
                            list()))

Finding this was important to me because I was using one function to build model definitions into a wrapper around inla, and I was stumped for a while as to why my code worked during interactive debugging but not with function calls!

I hope others find this helpful, and I'm glad to give back to this excellent support group.

--Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm attempting to fit a Gamma Family Mixed Effects model in INLA.

The model summary indicates that INLA is significantly over-fitting the data.

This leads me to believe that I might want to tune the prior for precision of this Gamma model.  The INLA doc for the Gamma family describes the linear predictor lined to mu as exp(eta).  This makes sense.  Then it describes the hyperparameter Phi which is exp(Theta) as the precision parameter, but isn't very clear on how to interpret it.

A very simple model with only one Random Effect produces: "Precision parameter for the Gamma observations 7811.962" (The mean)

However, I'm not clear how to interpret this, as it is not a simple to understand parameter like the Gaussian Model.

Two specific questions:

1) How to interpret  Theta in the Gama model family in INLA

2) Advice for how to estimate some reasonable informative prior for the Gamma model, and some ways that I might tune it in INLA

Thank You!

I have a model with some nested Random Effectts.

Faraway has a nice example that I'm attempting to understand a bit more:  http://www.maths.bath.ac.uk/~jjf23/inla/nested.html

In his model, Faraway describes the data as having three RE: Lab, Technician, Sample.

He creates a two levels of labels in R

eggs$labtech <- factor(paste0(eggs$Lab,eggs$Technician))
eggs$labtechsamp <- factor(paste0(eggs$Lab,eggs$Technician,eggs$Sample))

Then, his model includes the RE as "layers" including groups and sub-groups:

formula <- Fat ~ 1 + f(Lab, model="iid") + f(labtech, model="iid") + f(labtechsamp, model="iid")

This is where I'm confused.  The combined label of "labtechsamp" is unique for each grouping of data.  That makes sense.  But then, he also has the larger groups included for "lab" and "labtech".

Is this standard practice for nested models?  To have each level of grouping be a factor.
(Note: For my model, I don't care about the RE values.  I just want to account for the effects on the outcome variable.)

Thank You!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Bug in multiple likelihood demo
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Bug in multiple likelihood demo
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Mike, for your email.

Agree, it is important to know how 'data.frame' expand a matrix, like

> Y=matrix(1:6,2,3)
> data.frame(Y)
  X1 X2 X3
1  1  3  5
2  2  4  6

which is a little counter-intuitive compared to the case where y is a
vector where the name is kept

> y = 1:3
> data.frame(y)
  y
1 1
2 2
3 3

if we give it a name

> data.frame(Y=Y)
  Y.1 Y.2 Y.3
1   1   3   5
2   2   4   6

is use that name to get Y.1 Y.2 ...

usually, if I do not have just vectors of equal length, I will use
'list' instead, like

> list(Y=Y, y=y)
$Y
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6

$y
[1] 1 2 3

which you can pass as the 'data' argument

Another issue to be aware about, is that the length is expanded, like

> y = 1
> Y
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6
> data.frame(Y,y)
  X1 X2 X3 y
1  1  3  5 1
2  2  4  6 1

I'll update the example on the web-page; thx.

H

> .  Specifically, it appears to me that the demo assumes intermediate

> variables are still present in the environment, even if the inla call
> looks like it only needs the final data.frame.
>
> Here's the first example above, verbatim:
>
> ##  Simple linear regression with observations with two different
> ##  variances.
> n = 100
> N = 2*n
> y = numeric(N)
> x = rnorm(N)
>

> y[1:n + n] = 1 + x[1:n + n] + rnorm(n, sd = 1/sqrt(2))
>
> Y = matrix(NA, N, 2)
> Y[1:n, 1] = y[1:n]
> Y[1:n + n, 2] = y[1:n + n]
>
> formula = Y ~ x + 1
> result = inla(
>         formula,
>         data = data.frame(Y, x),
>         family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
>         control.family = list(list(prior = "flat", param =
> numeric()),
>                             list()))
>
> This runs as expected.
>
> However, if you run it again with a few small changes that seem like
> they shouldn't matter, I get an error:
>
> ##  Simple linear regression with observations with two different
> ##  variances.
> n = 100
> N = 2*n
> y = numeric(N)
> x = rnorm(N)
>
> y[1:n] = 1 + x[1:n] + rnorm(n, sd = 1/sqrt(1))
> y[1:n + n] = 1 + x[1:n + n] + rnorm(n, sd = 1/sqrt(2))
>
> Y = matrix(NA, N, 2)
> Y[1:n, 1] = y[1:n]
> Y[1:n + n, 2] = y[1:n + n]
>
> df = data.frame(Y, x)
>
> remove(Y)

> formula = Y ~ x + 1
> result = inla(
>         formula,
>         data = df,
>         family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
>         control.family = list(list(prior = "flat", param =
> numeric()),
>                             list()))
>
> Error in eval(parse(text = formula[2]), data) : object 'Y' not found
>
>
> The issue is that the formula doesn't know how to find "Y" because
> there is no "Y" in the df data.frame, but rather two columns, "X.1"
> and "X.2" that are autogenerated from Y.  (It's not better if you do
> df = data.frame(Y=Y,x=x) as you end up with "Y.1" and "Y.2").  The
> fact that the original example runs tells me that formula is finding
> Y in the global environment and not through the data = df part of the
> inla call.
>
> A fix that works is to change the formula to formula = cbind(Y.1,Y.2)
> ~ x + 1.  Full working example below:
>
> ##  Simple linear regression with observations with two different
> ##  variances.
> n = 100
> N = 2*n
> y = numeric(N)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Advice for tuning prior of Gamma Mixed Effects Model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Advice for tuning prior of Gamma Mixed Effects Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the gamma model uses the Constant coefficient of variation
parameterisation, where Var() = E()^2 * constant, or Prec() = 1/E()^2 *
prec.parameter

and you estimate the prec.parameter.  see inla.doc("gamma")

I havn't computed the PC-prior for this case, which would be the
'correct' default choice, and I expect that the default prior is no
good for you data and gives you overfitting.

would the prior pc.prec  do better?  Again, the PC-prior case should
computed and implemented. Its also possible for formulate Gamma
regression using Var() = E() * ... , which could be an alternative

Best
H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Nested Random effects
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Nested Random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

INLA is very very simple in the representation and have no internal
notion, at all, of 'nested effects', or know about what is nested
within what. From a computational point of view, we do not need to and
it does not help to know, so...

with

y ~ -1 + f(i, model="iid") + f(j, model="iid")

then we simply give the linear predictor for y, as eta. with U as the
first effect (i), and V as the second effect (j), then this model
simply says

eta[1] = U[i[1]] + V[j[1]]
eta[2] = U[i[2]] + V[j[2]]
eta[3] = U[i[3]] + V[j[3]]

etc.

so its all about getting the indices right.

for the 'iid' model, then the index can also be a factor.

Best
H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial mixture multiscale models in R-INLA?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatial mixture multiscale models in R-INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Harry,

If I read the referred paper correctly, there is a
p*v term in the predictor, where both p and v are indexed over the regions. INLA cannot deal with the multiplication of 2 random effects of high dimension. One of them would have to be dimension 1-5 for this to work.

I think the proposed models would work if there was only one "p" for each y-variable (p same over the index).

There are of course many other possibilities for modeling regions and sub-regions in INLA. BYM2 would be one type of model component you could use for one or both levels.

I don't have any BYM2 examples myself, but look at the online resources and at the BYM paper(s) (and ask the authors).

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.subject: RE: [r-inla] Nested Random effects
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Nested Random effects
messages.body_plain:
It’s a clever way of getting to the same or at least a similar answer.

In my experience, the workhorse glmer tends to choke on this approach of (1|effect), (1|effect_label1), etc., and instead tends to assign all of the variance to one of the “effect” categories and zero out the others, which is almost certainly wrong. Varying slopes may be necessary, which is time-consuming for a data set of any significant size, or perhaps you could just impose covariance priors with a package like blme and get it to work.

But INLA handles this formulation with aplomb, even with larger data sets, as long as you follow the usual guidance to keep the number of total groups at a manageable number (e.g., stay below double digits). Whether it works because the fully-Bayesian approach avoids boundary problems, or because of the robustness of the estimation method, or both, I do not know, but it is great to see.

Jonathan

messages.body_plain:
Yes, the INLA formulation is more general and do not rely on the
concept of 'random effects' like glmer. an iid random effect is just a
special case of a Gaussian component, and the important feature is the
Markov structure which makes it computational efficient; and of'course
less neigbours means higher computational efficiency.

H

Depends on the specific model you want, of course, but I would usually also use the parent levels.
E.g. school, class, student: the class wide performance is something you want to explicitly model (even when modelling student level performance) because it can depends on the teacher or the classroom facilities. Similarly, the school level can be a proxy for resources or general student background.

Haakon

Hi, I am trying to modell runoff with the SPDE approach. I have bout point observations of runoff and precipitation, at the same location.

I have made an SPDE model only containing my point-observations of runoff, it has been done as following:

SPDE <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha = 2)

A = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh,
                     loc=data.matrix(df[ , c('locx', 'locy')]))

formula <- y ~ -1 + intercept + f(spatial_field, model = SPDE)

output <- inla(formula, family = "gaussian",
                       data = list(y = df_pred$y, intercept = rep(1, SPDE$n.spde),
                                   spatial_field = 1:SPDE$n.spde),
                       control.predictor = list(A = A, compute = TRUE))

Now I would like to expand this model into a model where I have precipitation as a spatially varying coefficient. How would I do this?

Hope someone have time to help me! I would really appreciate it!
Ida

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am running a model, the 'graph' parameter is specified using a .dat file, I have 20 spatial locations, each location has one or two neighbors, and this error popped up when running inla():

      <simpleError in if (n.from.graph <= 0) {    stop(paste("Argument 'n from graph' is void:", n.from.graph))}: can't specify Null when TRUE/FALSE is required

my model is like:

    formula.ST1 <- y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6 + X7 + X8 + X9 +
      f(ID.area, model="besag",graph="/Users/.../adj.dat") +
      f(ID.year, model="rw1") +
      f(ID.year1, model="iid")

    lcs.train <- inla.make.lincombs(ID.year = diag(actualPeriodNeeded-stepahead),
                                    ID.year1 = diag(actualPeriodNeeded-stepahead))

    ST1 <- inla(formula.ST1,family="gaussian",data=data,
                                 control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                                 control.compute=list(cpo=TRUE, dic=TRUE),
                                 lincomb=lcs.train)

I have 20 locations, so n should not be <= 0 right? So I don't really understand what does it mean and how to fix it, can anyone please help me? Thanks!

Chris

messages.subject: Problem doing linear combinations with grouped random effects
messages.subject_clean: Problem doing linear combinations with grouped random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to calculate the linear combination of complex sum of random fields, and one fixed-effect factor, and am having problems with the grouping.

First, the factor, as a lead up to the harder problem. For my (and hopefully others) future benefit, inla choked on implementing a linear combination with a factor when coded in a naive way, but I found this old post were you explained that the factors have to be expanded: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/IaTSakB7qy4. Doing so fixed the factor problem.   An example below, modified from the example in that thread:

formula = y ~ x + z + w - 1

y=1:3
x = as.factor(c("a", "b", "a"))
z = c(1, 2, 2)
w = rnorm(3)
df = data.frame(x=x,y=y,z=z)

r = inla(formula , data = df)

For the linear combination, I want the sum of x and z. The naive way to write the lc doesn't work:

lc = inla.make.lincombs(x=x,z=z)

r = inla(formula, data = df, lincomb = lc, verbose = TRUE)

> *** ERROR *** Section no [0] named [x] in file [30338400] offset[ 0] is unknown.

because inla expands factor names as:

rownames(r$summary.fixed)
[1] "xa" "xb" "z" "w"

Instead, we need

lc = inla.make.lincombs(xa=c(1,NA,1),xb=c(NA,1,NA),z=z)

r = inla(formula, data = df, lincomb = lc, verbose = TRUE)

and all is well.

After implementing that fix to the factor, I got one step further into my inla call and encountered a similar error:

formula = y ~ x + f(geoRow, model = 'iid', constr=TRUE, group=timeRow, control.group=list(model = 'rw2'))

lc = inla.make.lincombs(xa=c(1,NA,1),xb=c(NA,1,NA),geoRow=c(1,2,3),timeRow=c(1,1,2)))  # simple illustration: real data has many more rows

r = inla(..., verbose = TRUE)

> ...
  section=[26] name=[lincomb.lc001] type=[LINCOMB]
	  inla_parse_lincomb...
		secname = [lincomb.lc001]
		filename [C:/Users/mfamulare/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpctjwwQ/file3ab02a9c2bde/data.files/file3ab042d44aab]
		file.offset [0]
		precision [1e+009]
		Open file [C:/Users/mfamulare/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpctjwwQ/file3ab02a9c2bde/data.files/file3ab042d44aab] at location [0]
		Number of sections [10]
			Section [0] is named [geoRow]
			Section has offset=[1728] and n=[288]
			npairs=[1]
			Section [1] is named [timeRow]

*** ERROR *** 	Section no [1] named [timeRow] in file [91108000] offset[               0] is unknown.

Based on the logic of the factor error, this implies that I need to explicitly build out the whole interaction matrix with column names like c("geoRow1timeRow1", "geoRow2timeRow1", ... "geoRow1timeRow2" ... ) and have NA in all but one column of an enormous matrix.  Is that true???  Or is there another way to specify the linear combinations? Or do I have probably another bug?

Barring a better solution, my plan at the moment is to just to add some rows to the original input data.frame that zero out all the covariates I don't want the linear combinations to, so that the summary.fitted.values are just the result of the combined random fields.  This will work for my particular use case at the moment, since I want the linear combination over all fields, but it is not a general solution.

As always, help will be appreciated!

Thanks,

--Mike

messages.subject_clean: Error: inla.uncbind not in namespace?
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

Tangentially related to my last question about linear combinations of grouped random effects <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/_e2C2L7Wc30>, I get an error when trying to use inla.uncbind that indicates that inla.cbind isn't exported to the INLA namespace.

If I run the example here <http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-I-have-some-linear-combinations-of-the-nodes-in-the-latent-field-that-I-want-to-compute-the-posterior-marginal-of-is-that-possible->:

m = 10
wa = runif(m)
wb = runif(m)

## if 'wa' and 'wb' is defined in a matrix, like
A = cbind(a=wa, b=wb)

## then we can define the same lincombs using inla.uncbind(),
lc.many = inla.make.lincombs( inla.uncbind(A) )

I get
Error in inla.uncbind(A) : could not find function "inla.uncbind"

And explicitly calling INLA::inla.uncbind yields

lc.many = inla.make.lincombs( inla.uncbind(A) )

Error: 'inla.uncbind' is not an exported object from 'namespace:INLA'

I see inla.uncbind in the source <https://bitbucket.org/hrue/r-inla/src/c11a38115e38a849edae8adeb078a404b03840a8/rinla/R/lincomb.R?at=default&fileviewer=file-view-default#lincomb.R-181>, but I'm not sure why it isn't exported to the namespace.  I have no reason to think this issue is local to my machine, but one never knows.  Any idea how to fix?

My workaround at the moment is

lc1 <- do.call('inla.make.lincombs', as.list( as.data.frame(A)) )

which produces the same output as

lc2 <- inla.make.lincombs(a=wa,b=wb)

My session info:
R version 3.5.2 (2018-12-20)
Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 (64-bit)
Running under: Windows >= 8 x64 (build 9200)
INLA version 18.07.12

Thanks!

--Mike

messages.subject: A question about prediction using inla()
messages.subject_clean: A question about prediction using inla()
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I want to do spatio-temporal prediction using inla(), suppose I have two datasets:

First one with y values from time period 3 set to NA for prediction:

   x1  x2  y   time_period
1  4   3   5.32      1
2  6   6   3.65      1
3  4   2   8.74      2
4  6   8   3.64      2
5  4   2   na        3
6  6   7   na        3

The second dataset has the same x1 and x2 columns but with y values from time periods 3 and 4 set to NA:

   x1  x2  y   time_period
1  4   3   5.32      1
2  6   6   3.65      1
3  4   2   8.74      2
4  6   8   3.64      2
5  4   2   na        3
6  6   7   na        3
7  4   5   na        4
8  6   9   na        4

If I run the model using these two datasets separately, will the prediction values for time period 3 from these two model results be the same? And why?

Thanks!

Chris

I have binomial data (number of "successes" and "failures") for 1955 counties, and I would like to predict the missed 1154 counties and plot them on the US map.

> spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh, alpha = 2)
> field.indices <- inla.spde.make.index("field", n.spde = spde$n.spde)
>
> proj_grid <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh, xlim = range(pl.bound$loc[, 1]), ylim = range(pl.bound$loc[, 2]), dims = nxy)
>
> A.est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, loc=coo)                                        ### coo - coords for available data
> A.pred <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, loc=coop)                                      ### coop - coords for unavailable data
> stack.est <- inla.stack(data = list(y = df$r, numtrials = df$n),                     ### r - number of successes, n - total number of cases (successes + failures).
>   A = list(A.est, 1), effects = list(c(field.indices, list(Intercept=1)),
>     list(stco = df$stco)), tag="est")                                                ### stco - county code
>
> stack.pred <- inla.stack(data = list(y = df$r, numtrials = df$n),                    ### df$r and df$n are NA
>   A = list(A.pred, 1), effects = list(c(field.indices, list(Intercept=1)),
>     list(stco = df$stco)), tag="pred")
>
> stack <- inla.stack(stack.est, stack.pred)
> formula = y ~ -1 + Intercept + f(stco, model="iid", param=c(0.001,0.001)) + f(field, model=spde)
>
> res <- inla(formula, data = inla.stack.data(stack, spde = spde), family = "binomial", Ntrials = numtrials, control.predictor= list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE, link=inla.stack.data(stack)$link))
>
I have a problem with extracting of the linear predictor values (or another summary) on the mesh.

> xy.in <http://xy.in> <- inout(proj_grid$lattice$loc, pl.bound$loc)
> g.mean2 <- inla.mesh.project(proj_grid, res$summary.linear.predictor$mean[pred.ind])
> g.sd2 <- inla.mesh.project(proj_grid, res$summary.linear.predictor$sd[pred.ind])
> g.mean2[!xy.in] <- g.sd2[!xy.in] <- NA
>
> trellis.par.set(regions=list(col=terrain.colors(16)))
> grid.arrange(levelplot(g.mean2, scales=list(draw=F), xlab='', ylab='', main='mean'),
> levelplot(g.sd2, scal=list(draw=F), xla='', yla='', main='sd'), nrow = 2)             ### How can I add the borders of counties? Thnx.

Can somebody help me with this issue?
PS: Can I plot both estimated and predicted values on the map?

Thank you in advance.
Garry

messages.body_plain:
The A matrix you use in stack.pred uses points commented as being point for unavailabledata, but if you want to index using only those point you won’t get the entire field. You could make the prediction stack predict at all mesh nodes, regardless of whether they have data or not. That would allow the inla.mesh.project/or code to work properly.
Alternatively, to save space, extract further indexing information from your current stack, relating to both est and pred, that together would give you all of the locations.

Finn

messages.subject: Using A matrix with automatic intercept / intercepts and factor variables
messages.subject_clean: Using A matrix with automatic intercept / intercepts and factor variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a question regarding the handling of intercepts, A-matrices, and factor variables in inla.

If you try to fit a model with an A matrix in control.predictor without removing the automatic intercept from the formula, you get a warning message like:
##... : The A-matrix in the predictor (see ?control.predictor)
is specified
## but an intercept is in the formula. This will likely result
## in the intercept being applied multiple times in the model, and is likely
## not what you want. See ?inla.stack for more information.
## You can remove the intercept adding “-1” to the formula.
I am a bit confused by this error message -- it says that it is *likely* that the intercept is applied multiple times but does not say whether it actually is. Is there any way to check if it actually is applied more than once? And if it is, is there any way to prevent it? I do not have any manual intercept in the model, so there should be no issue coming from that.

The above is my main question, but for some context:
The examples I have seen solve this warning by removing the automatic intercept with "-1" and then manually creating an intercept covariate. However, this does not seem to work in my case. I'll explain what I am trying to do in case my whole approach is wrong somehow.
I am trying to fit a model along the lines of
y ~ 1 + a + b + f(...) + f(...)
where a,b are categorical variables, and the f:s are rw2 and spde models with some replicates that I control with the A-matrix. Since a,b are factors I expect one level from each to be dropped to prevent identification/colinearity problems. This works just fine when the automatic intercept is included in the formula, but when I instead create a manual intercept and drop the automatic one it doesn't: all levels of a are kept. This seems to give problems with very large uncertainties in the estimates. Because of this it seems natural to me to use the automatic intercept, but this of course gives the warning above.

Here are some excerpts from the fixed effects estimates, where we see this phenomenon, note the very large sds for a with the manual intercept, and that level a1 is included.

messages.subject: Define effects relative to baseline
messages.subject_clean: Define effects relative to baseline
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Is it possible to "derive" coefficients relative to a baseline value, so that we get a distribution with a value?

Consider the following:

C = count of organism (response)
season = categorical predictor (1,...,4)
cover = continuous predictor

This is how I would specify it in bugs:

    model {

    # Priors
    for (i in 1:n.group){
    alpha[i] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)    # seasons
    beta[i] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01) # seasons:cover
    }

    # Likelihood
    for (i in 1:n) {
    C[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    log(lambda[i]) <- alpha[season[i]] + beta[season[i]]*cover[i]
    }

    # Define effects relative to baseline level
    eff.winter <- alpha[1]      # Winter effect on count data
    eff.spring <- alpha[2] - alpha[1] # Spring effect
    eff.summer <- alpha[3] - alpha[1  # Summer effect
    eff.fall   <- alpha[4] - alpha[1] # Fall effect
    eff.win.cover  <- beta[1]  # Effect of cover during winter season
    eff.spr.cover  <- beta[2] - beta[1]  # Slope spring:cover
    eff.sum.cover  <- beta[3] - beta[1]  # Slope summer:cover
    eff.fall.cover <- beta[4] - beta[1]  # Slope fall:cover

    }

This model can be easily achieved in INLA using:

inla(C ~ season*cover, data = ..., family = ...)

A slightly more complicated but version I prefer to use is this:

#organize data

n.loc = max(as.numeric(inla.data$season))

inla.data$i.int <http://i.int> <- as.numeric(inla.data$season)

inla.data$j.int <http://j.int> <-  as.numeric(inla.data$season) + n.loc

inla.data$k.int <http://k.int> = inla.data$j.int <http://j.int> + n.loc

form = C ~ -1 + cover + f(i.int <http://i.int>,model = 'iid2d', n = 2*n.loc) + f(j.int <http://j.int>, cover, copy = 'i.int <http://i.int>')

I3 <- inla(form, family = "poisson", data = inla.data,
           control.compute = list(waic = T))

When using this form, the effects are relative to the baseline factor (in this case winter). I can subtract the baseline from the mean and get back 'truth', but then my uncertainty with the estimate doesn't follow this "derived" value. So, as I did in BUGS (e.g., alpha[3] - alpha[1]), is it possible to derive relative effects in INLA?

Thanks for your help,
Brent

messages.subject: Map genetic sub-group of cohort with incomplete testing.
messages.subject_clean: Map genetic sub-group of cohort with incomplete testing.
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA experts,

The background: We have a set of about 2,250 cases from a population disease register, and combining with census data have produced maps via the BYM model. For about 50% of cases we have data regarding testing a specific gene that causes about 10% of the cases. So out of 2,250 cases, about 1000 were genetically tested and roughly 100 tested +ve with 900 -ve. The people who got tested are probably spatially biased to be living closer to research centres. I have been asked to produce a map of spatial incidence of where this gene occurs (if possible). However I don't know how to do this given not every case was tested.

Is there any clever way of using inla to produce such a map? Although I have been working with the BYM model I'm wondering could I treat data as point patterns for this purpose. For example I see in the spde book section 4.3 geostatistics under preferential sampling. Could the preferential sampling approach be adapted to point pattern data instead of geostatistics?

I appreciate any thoughts folks might have.
Thanks,
James

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Map genetic sub-group of cohort with incomplete testing.
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Map genetic sub-group of cohort with incomplete testing.
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Your issue looks very similar to the types of models used in ecology for transect sampling, where the probability of observing an animal depends on its distance to the observer.  Such models tend to lead to nonlinear predictor models that can’t be run directly in inla, but can be defined and estimated in the inlabru package (which was developed partly for this precise reason).  In the workshop tutorial material on inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> we look at Poisson point process models, with observation models modulated by detection probability models.
I’m not sure your problem would be best described using Poisson process formalism, but the same idea can be applied for measurements (0/1 detection indicators) observed at fixed locations.  The other preferential sampling modelling techniques might also be combined with this; if you can formulate a model for the data-generation process, it would be easier to figure out what implementation approach would be suitable.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Hierarchical model including diagnostic uncertainty
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Hierarchical model including diagnostic uncertainty
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

it depends on the details of the model, so an example (showing more
precisely what model you would like) might help.

For a thinned Poisson process (as an actual point process) one can do
that in INLA if the log of the thinning probability is linear in some
latent Gaussian variable, or just needs a positive scaling factor,
e.g. a model of the type
 eta = log(lambda(x)) + log(p(z;beta))
 y ~ Poisson process with intensity exp(eta) (which is the thinned
version of lambda).
log p(z) can be beta * z^2, with beta positive, via the "clinear" model.

For more complicated thinning probability models, where log(p(z))
isn't linear in parameters beta, the inlabru package can be used
instead (inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org>).
There one can do models such as log p(z) =
exp(-abs(z/exp(beta1))^exp(beta2)) that aren't linear in beta1 and
beta2.

Finn

Not sure about the details, but
1) the A matrix used in the stack needs to be computed for the data locations used in each individual call to inla.
2) I generally recommend agains using data dependent meshes in loops. It’s much safer to build one mesh and use that (unless each inla call is for a different region)
Based on the domain of interest instead of the data locations.

If the problem is reproduced every time you run the code, then add some print statements before the inla call that breaks, printing the R object structures, to identify precisely what went wrong.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Error in inla()
messages.body_plain:
I’d recommend having only one mesh.
The data locations and prediction locations etc do not need to have any relation to the mesh nodes; they just need to lie within the mesh domain.
While adapting the mesh to the data locations is sometimes useful to reduce model size, it isn’t very practical to have several meshes for the same domain. It’s much more practical to have a single mesh with high enough resolution to be able to define the spatial model in all the different data settings.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the late repply.

My problem was just a comma....

when stacking, what is very important is the data, not where you take
the data. That is, I used a data frame (several dataframes actually)
to store the data. So when I call the column where the prescence are
stored I REALLY CALL THE WHOLE COLUMN (the header included). Since
this header is a Character string, the INLA.STACK cannot compute
between numeric and characters... All I needed was to add a comma
between the brackets to call just the data, not the whole column.

Then my code ended from

  stk.cost <- inla.stack(
  data=list(y=costeros[[i]][8]),   <---------------- the problem
  A=list(A,1), tag=colnames(costeros[[3]][8]),
  effects=list(list(s=1:spde$n.spde),
               data.frame(Intercept=1,
                          TS=inla.group(costeros[[i]][,3]),
                          SS=inla.group(costeros[[i]][,4]),
                          BZ=inla.group(costeros[[i]][,5]))))
to this code

  stk.cost <- inla.stack(
  data=list(y=costeros[[i]][,8]),   <---------------- the "#$%&"#$%#"$%" comma
  A=list(A,1), tag=colnames(costeros[[3]][8]),
  effects=list(list(s=1:spde$n.spde),
               data.frame(Intercept=1,
                          TS=inla.group(costeros[[i]][,3]),
                          SS=inla.group(costeros[[i]][,4]),
                          BZ=inla.group(costeros[[i]][,5]))))

Thank you Finn for everything

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I suggest just using a manual intercept, then you know what is going on. There are ways to check what you are doing when you make automatic choices, but it is unneccesarily intricate compared to just defining your choices manually.

With factors, what I prefer to do is
1. for small factors, define the 0-1 equivalents manually myself
2. for larger factors (4+ levels) define an iid effect over the factor levels

For your problme, think about the manual intercept as the "baseline" for the factor. Then all the factor levels describe a change from this baseline. If you do not specify a random effect shrinkage (iid effect), or remove one factor level, your model does not make any sense.

How the defaults for factors and intercept combinations interact with stack is unknown to me, so I suggest setting it up manually and not relying on automatic expansions when using stack.

Best,
Haakon

On Sun, 14 Apr 2019 at 14:12, Erik Håkansson <erik...@gmail.com> wrote:

>

> ##... : The A-matrix in the predictor (see ?control.predictor)
> is specified
> ## but an intercept is in the formula. This will likely result
> ## in the intercept being applied multiple times in the model, and is likely
> ## not what you want. See ?inla.stack for more information.
> ## You can remove the intercept adding “-1” to the formula.
> I am a bit confused by this error message -- it says that it is *likely* that the intercept is applied multiple times but does not say whether it actually is. Is there any way to check if it actually is applied more than once? And if it is, is there any way to prevent it? I do not have any manual intercept in the model, so there should be no issue coming from that.
>
